title: What consumers want from direct mail in a tight economy
summary: Direct mail means more when consumers take longer to decide. Learn what makes people keep and share direct mail and how marketers use that information.
body_markdown:
Consumer needs are shifting. In fact, 84% of consumers say rising prices have changed the way they shop in 2026.


In our recent[State of Direct Mail: Consumer Insights 2026](https://www.lob.com/state-of-direct-mail/consumer-insights/2026-report) , consumers revealed how the economy is changing how they interact with direct mail. They’re waiting for sales, comparing offers, researching alternatives, and holding onto mail longer.


So what should marketers do differently? The data points to three shifts.


## **1. Consumers are taking longer to decide**


People are more deliberate about purchases right now. That makes direct mail valuable beyond the moment of conversion: it can help shoppers research, compare, and come back when they’re ready.


Among economically strained consumers, 87% have taken action after receiving direct mail, compared with 67% of consumers less affected by rising prices.


**What this means for marketers:**


- **Help people evaluate, not just convert.** Include comparisons, product details, pricing tiers, financing information, eligibility, or other information that makes the decision easier.
- **Rethink urgency.** Give people a reason to return to the piece rather than relying entirely on “ACT NOW” messaging. There are more effective ways to[create urgency](https://www.lob.com/blog/how-to-create-urgency-in-direct-mail-offers-that-convert) for deliberate shoppers.
- **Make delayed conversion easy.** Use[QR codes](https://www.lob.com/blog/track-direct-mail-using-qr-codes) and[PURLs](https://www.lob.com/blog/purl-campaign-tracking-how-to-measure-every-mail-interaction) so people can pick the journey back up later.


## **2. Useful mail earns a longer life**


Nearly 9 in 10 consumers say relevance influences whether they take action on direct mail. And when people are watching their budgets, “relevant” increasingly means **useful** . The[customer data you use](https://www.lob.com/blog/what-customer-data-actually-improves-direct-mail-response-rates) determines whether your mail hits that bar.


That could be a specific offer, but it could also be information they want to reference later: product comparisons, deadlines, pricing, a checklist, or next steps.


Direct mail also has a social life: 77% of economically strained consumers share mail, compared with 55% of consumers less affected by rising prices.


**What this means for marketers:**


- **Lead with concrete value.** “Save $75” gives someone more to work with than “exclusive savings.”
- **Create something worth keeping.** Think reference guides, calendars, comparison charts, checklists, or longer-lasting offers.
- **Design for sharing.** Make the key message and value proposition easy for someone to hand to a spouse, colleague, parent, or other decision-maker. Strong[direct mail design](https://www.lob.com/ebooks/thumb-stopping-mail) makes this easier.


## **3. The response may happen somewhere else and later**


If consumers are researching more and taking longer to purchase, immediate direct response tells only part of the story. That's where[cross-channel attribution](https://www.lob.com/blog/what-is-cross-channel-attribution-and-how-does-direct-mail-fit-in) becomes essential.


A mailpiece might prompt someone to search the brand, visit a store, scan a QR code days later, or[return to a purchase](https://www.lob.com/blog/the-role-of-direct-mail-in-modern-retargeting-campaigns) they were already considering.


**What this means for marketers:**


- **Give people multiple paths forward.** QR codes, PURLs, search-friendly messaging, store information, and clear CTAs let consumers respond however they prefer.
- **Connect mail to the rest of the journey.** Take an[omnichannel approach](https://www.lob.com/content/omnichannel-marketing) that coordinates direct mail with email, SMS, paid media, and other follow-up.
- **Measure beyond the first response.** Look at downstream web visits, branded search, store visits, and[delayed conversions](https://www.lob.com/blog/how-to-measure-direct-mail-and-why-one-signal-isnt-enough) —not just immediate scans or purchases.


## **Direct mail for a more deliberate consumer**


A tighter economy doesn’t necessarily mean consumers stop engaging. It means they’re more selective about what deserves their attention and what helps them make a decision.


For marketers, that makes the opportunity less about sending louder promotions and more about creating mail that is relevant enough to keep, useful enough to share, and easy to act on when the time is right.
